newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam set to welcome Hashimoto with open arms.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam set to welcome Hashimoto with open arms.

text.p: Vietnam put the finishing touches on preparations to fete Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday, pledging closer links with its biggest aid donor, main trading partner and huge source of investment.

Official media reports ahead of Hashimoto's arrival in Hanoi on Saturday were peppered with the words "cooperation" and "friendship" and a giant poster bearing the Japanese flag was erected outside the presidential palace.

"This visit to Vietnam will offer an opportunity for leaders of the two countries to discuss orientations and measures to promote further all-round relations into the 21st century," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
In a letter to the Vietnamese people ahead of his visit, Hashimoto was just as warm. He spoke of uniting hearts and joining forces to build a better world for future generations.

Hashimoto, on a swing through Southeast Asia that has so far taken him to Brunei, Malaysia and Indonesia, will meet Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet and Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi before leaving on Sunday for Singapore.
His tour was in doubt because of the hostage crisis in Peru, where Marxist rebels still hold 74 captives at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
However, he has been kept in constant touch with Tokyo and Peru during his tour and a Japanese embassy official in Jakarta said on Friday that rumours of a schedule change were unfounded.
Relations between Japan and Vietnam have gone from strength to strength since Hanoi embarked on reform along market lines and opened doors to the outside world 10 years ago.

Many older Vietnamese have bad memories of Japan's World War Two occupation of their country, which has been blamed for a devastating famine from 1943 to 1945. But that era is rarely mentioned by politicians from either country these days.
Japan is now the leading donor of official development aid (ODA) to Vietnam, pledging $3.23 billion between 1992 and 1996.

It is Vietnam's biggest trading partner. Some $3.0 billion worth of goods and services were traded between the two countries last year, accounting for about one-sixth of Vietnam's combined import and export volume.
Hanoi's 1995 trade surplus with Japan was about $750 million.
Japanese companies have earmarked some $2.7 billion for investment projects, placing their nation second in a growing list of countries looking for a share in Vietnam's economic boom.

Masaaki Miyashita, Minister of the Japanese Embassy in Hanoi, said Hashimoto would probably encourage Vietnam to improve the environment for foreign investors and may touch on the question of how to quicken the now-glacial pace of ODA disbursement.
However, he said that since Vietnam joined the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 1995, Tokyo wanted to broaden relations beyond the economic sphere.
"Until now, it has been a donor and recipient relationship. Now the situation is changing," he said.
Miyashita said other areas of cooperation were possible, including dialogue on regional security and an exchange of defence personnel.
